title: Transition to parenthood and postnatal mental wellbeing
blurb: Support bonding and the move into parenthood, tell baby blues from depression and psychosis, and use the Whooley and GAD-2 questions to decide when to refer (NICE CG192, NG194).
question: On day 10, Leila, 30, tells the community midwife she has felt low and tearful since day 3, takes no pleasure in anything, and feels she is a bad mother. Her partner says she is not sleeping even when the baby sleeps. Is this baby blues, and what should the midwife do?

teach.body: Formally: the transition to parenthood is the psychological, emotional and social adjustment to caring for a baby, including forming a secure emotional attachment (NMC SPM 3.17.3). In plain English: tiredness, a new identity, recovery from birth and a changed relationship all arrive at once. Most parents adapt with support, but some develop mental health problems that need recognising early. Suicide is the leading cause of maternal death from 6 weeks to 1 year after pregnancy (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).

items: Discuss bonding before and after the birth and the approaches that help.
Encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to the baby's cues.
Talk about what can make bonding harder: physical and emotional recovery, a traumatic birth, fatigue, feeding concerns, demands of parenthood.
Recognise parents who may need more support: care-experienced parents, adverse childhood experiences, traumatic birth, complex psychosocial needs.
Involve her partner according to her wishes (1.1.3), and offer the chance to talk about her birth experience at each contact (1.2.5).

rows.label: Features
values: Low mood, no enjoyment, guilt, hopelessness

rows.label: Response
values: Assess, refer to GP or MH

teach.caption: NHS: baby blues usually go within 2 weeks; postpartum psychosis affects about 1 in 1,000 women and is a medical emergency.

steps.label: Whooley questions
steps.sub: low mood? loss of interest? (past month)

steps.label: GAD-2
steps.sub: nervous or on edge? can't stop worrying? (2 weeks)

steps.label: Positive or concern
steps.sub: EPDS or PHQ-9, or refer to GP

steps.label: Severe
steps.sub: refer to a mental health professional

teach.caption: Ask both at booking and early postnatal; consider at all later contacts. GAD-2 score of 3 or more: GAD-7 or refer to GP.

children.label: Likely baby blues: support and review
Assess (Whooley, EPDS); refer to GP or MH

teach.caption: Thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby: urgent assessment the same day; 999 if immediate danger.

teach.h: Who is at highest risk of psychosis?
teach.body: Be alert for possible postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth in women with a past or present severe mental illness (such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia) or a family history of severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative. If psychosis is suspected, refer to a secondary mental health service, preferably a specialist perinatal service, for assessment within 4 hours of referral. Admission within 12 months of birth should normally be to a mother and baby unit.

items.label: assessment after referral for suspected psychosis
GAD-2 score: GAD-7 or GP referral

teach.body: Leila's low mood began on day 3 but is still present on day 10 and is worsening, with loss of pleasure, guilt and poor sleep even when the baby sleeps. These are features of depression, not baby blues. The midwife asks the Whooley questions (both positive), asks directly about thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby, and arranges further assessment such as the EPDS or referral to the GP, documenting and handing over to the health visitor. She reassures Leila that asking for help rarely leads to a baby being removed.

teach.text: Do not wait for baby blues to "pass" when the picture is getting worse. And do not confuse psychosis with severe depression: hallucinations, delusions, mania or confusion in the first 2 weeks are an EMERGENCY (assessment within 4 hours), not a GP appointment next week.

items: Support bonding: skin-to-skin, face-to-face interaction, responding to cues; involve the partner as she wishes.
Baby blues: first days, usually gone within 2 weeks; persisting or worsening low mood needs assessment.
Whooley plus GAD-2 at booking and early postnatal; positive: EPDS or PHQ-9 or GP referral.
Postpartum psychosis: sudden, first 2 weeks, about 1 in 1,000; assessment within 4 hours.
Partners can have postnatal depression too.

summary: You can now support parents through the transition to parenthood and promote bonding. You can tell baby blues from postnatal depression and postpartum psychosis, use the Whooley and GAD-2 questions, and refer with the right urgency.

A.q: Within what period do the baby blues usually resolve after the birth?
options: Within 48 hours
Within 6 weeks
Within 3 months
Within 2 weeks
A.why: NHS: feeling down, anxious or irritable for a few days after the birth is very common; the baby blues usually go within 2 weeks. If symptoms continue or worsen, she needs help.

whyNot.0: Baby blues often start around the third day, so 48 hours is too short.
whyNot.1: Symptoms lasting to 6 weeks are beyond baby blues and suggest depression.
whyNot.2: Mood problems lasting 3 months are not baby blues.

A.q: Which pair of questions does NICE CG192 recommend for identifying possible depression at booking and in the early postnatal period?
options: The GAD-7 questionnaire
The Whooley questions
The CAGE questions
The Mini-Mental State Examination
A.why: CG192 1.5.4: ask the Whooley questions about feeling down, depressed or hopeless and about little interest or pleasure in doing things, alongside the GAD-2.

whyNot.0: GAD-7 is used after a positive GAD-2 (score 3 or more), not as the depression screening pair.
whyNot.2: CAGE questions screen for alcohol misuse.
whyNot.3: The MMSE assesses cognition, not depression.

A.q: Which feature most strongly suggests postpartum psychosis rather than baby blues?
options: Hearing voices that are not there
Crying for no clear reason on day 4
Feeling irritable and anxious
Worrying about breastfeeding
A.why: NHS: postpartum psychosis features hallucinations, delusions, mania, low mood or confusion, usually starting suddenly within 2 weeks of birth; it is a medical emergency.

whyNot.1: Tearfulness around day 4 is typical of baby blues.
whyNot.2: Irritability and anxiety in the first days are common in baby blues.
whyNot.3: Feeding worries are common and are not a psychotic feature.

B.q: Rosa, 34, has bipolar disorder. On day 5 her partner reports she has barely slept, is talking very fast and believes the baby has been swapped. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange a GP appointment for this week
Advise rest and review at the next visit
Urgent referral for assessment within 4 hours
Complete an EPDS and refer to talking therapies
B.why: CG192 1.5.12: if postpartum psychosis is suspected, refer to a secondary mental health service (preferably specialist perinatal) for assessment within 4 hours. Delusions and mania after birth in a woman with bipolar disorder fit this.

whyNot.0: A routine GP appointment is too slow for suspected psychosis.
whyNot.1: Psychosis can worsen rapidly; waiting is unsafe.
whyNot.3: EPDS and talking therapies suit depression, not suspected psychosis.

B.q: At booking, Nia, 25, scores 4 on the GAD-2. What does NICE CG192 recommend next?
options: Use the GAD-7 or refer her to her GP
No action: a score under 6 is normal
Refer for assessment within 4 hours
Repeat the GAD-2 at 28 weeks
B.why: CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more on the GAD-2, consider using the GAD-7 scale for further assessment or refer her to her GP.

whyNot.1: A GAD-2 score of 3 or more is the threshold for further assessment.
whyNot.2: Assessment within 4 hours is for suspected postpartum psychosis.
whyNot.3: A positive screen needs action now, not repeat screening later.

B.q: Which practice should the midwife encourage to promote emotional attachment between parents and their newborn?
options: Settling the baby in a separate room early on
Feeding to a strict schedule from day 1
Leaving the baby to cry to build a routine
Face-to-face interaction and skin-to-skin
B.why: NG194 1.3.17: encourage parents to value time with their baby, including face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding appropriately to the baby's cues.

whyNot.0: Early separation does not promote attachment, and it conflicts with safer sleep advice.
whyNot.1: Responsive feeding to the baby's cues, not a strict schedule, supports attachment.
whyNot.2: Responding to the baby's cues, not leaving them to cry, promotes attachment.

C.q: Dan, the partner of Grace, 29, tells the health visitor at 5 weeks that since the birth he has felt hopeless, cannot sleep and avoids holding the baby. Grace is well. Which response is best?
options: Explain that postnatal depression does not affect partners
Recognise possible depression; encourage him to seek help
Advise him to wait until Grace's 6 to 8 week postnatal check
Tell him this is normal adjustment to fatherhood
C.why: NHS: fathers and partners can also have depression after having a baby. His symptoms need assessment, for example via his GP or NHS talking therapies.

whyNot.0: Partners can develop postnatal depression too.
whyNot.2: Grace's check is about her health; Dan needs his own assessment now.
whyNot.3: Hopelessness, insomnia and avoiding the baby are not normal adjustment and need help.

C.q: Amy, 27, whose sister had postpartum psychosis, is on day 6. She seems well. What should the midwife be alert for and when?
options: Signs of psychosis from 6 months after the birth
Depression starting after the 6 to 8 week check
Anxiety about feeding in the first year
Signs of psychosis in the first 2 weeks
C.why: CG192 1.5.11: be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth in women with a past or present severe mental illness or a family history in a first-degree relative.

whyNot.0: Postpartum psychosis usually starts suddenly in the first 2 weeks, not at 6 months.
whyNot.1: Depression can start at any time, but the specific alert for a first-degree family history is psychosis in the first 2 weeks.
whyNot.2: Feeding anxiety is common but is not the specific risk linked to her family history.

C.q: Kemi, 32, had an emergency caesarean after a long labour. On day 8 she says she keeps reliving the birth and cannot stop thinking about it. Her mood is otherwise fair. What should the midwife do?
options: Tell her that memories of the birth fade without any help
Advise her to avoid talking about the birth
Offer to talk about the birth and signpost support
Refer her for assessment within 4 hours
C.why: NG194 1.2.5: at each postnatal contact give the woman the opportunity to talk about her birth experience and provide information about support and birth reflection services, following CG192 on traumatic birth.

whyNot.0: Dismissing her distress misses possible trauma symptoms that may need support.
whyNot.1: Avoidance is not advised; she should be offered the chance to talk about it.
whyNot.3: 4-hour assessment is for suspected psychosis; she needs support and appropriate follow-up.

reteach.title: Time, trend and type
reteach.question: Three questions sort most postnatal mood problems: when did it start, is it getting better or worse, and what kind of symptoms are they?

blocks.h: Ask about time, trend and type
blocks.body: TIME: baby blues start in the first days; depression can start any time in the first year; psychosis starts suddenly, usually in the first 2 weeks. TREND: blues get better within 2 weeks; depression persists; psychosis gets worse fast. TYPE: tearfulness and worry suggest blues; loss of enjoyment, guilt and hopelessness suggest depression; hallucinations, delusions, mania or confusion suggest psychosis.

blocks.text: "Baby blues" is a diagnosis of the first 2 weeks. Low mood that is still there or worsening after 2 weeks is not blues.

explain.body: Encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to cues. Talk about challenges: recovery, traumatic birth, fatigue, feeding concerns. Some parents need extra support, for example care-experienced parents or those with adverse childhood experiences.

test.q: Which parent does NG194 identify as possibly needing additional support with bonding?
options: A parent who had a planned home birth
A parent who has chosen to formula feed
A parent who grew up in the care system
A parent who is having a second baby
test.why: NG194 1.3.19: parents who have been through the care system, have experienced adverse childhood events, had a traumatic birth, or have complex psychosocial needs may need additional bonding support.

whyNot.0: Place of birth is not on the NG194 list.
whyNot.1: Feeding method is not a listed reason for additional bonding support.
whyNot.3: Having a second baby is not on the NG194 list.

explain.body: Whooley: in the past month, often bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless? Little interest or pleasure in doing things? GAD-2: in the past 2 weeks, feeling nervous, anxious or on edge? Not being able to stop or control worrying? Ask at booking and early postnatal.

test.q: What period do the Whooley questions ask the woman to think about?
options: The past month
The past 2 weeks
The past 24 hours
Since booking
test.why: The Whooley questions ask: "During the past month, have you often been bothered by..." (CG192 1.5.4).

whyNot.1: The past 2 weeks is the GAD-2 timeframe.
whyNot.2: A 24-hour window is not used in the Whooley questions.
whyNot.3: The questions refer to the past month, not since booking.

explain.body: Symptoms include low mood, loss of enjoyment, hopelessness, guilt, anxiety, poor sleep even when able to rest, poor concentration, difficulty bonding, and thoughts of suicide or harm. It can start in pregnancy or up to a year after birth. Treatment includes talking therapies and antidepressants, many of which are compatible with breastfeeding.

test.q: Up to how long after the birth can postnatal depression begin?
options: 2 weeks
1 year
6 weeks
3 months
test.why: NHS: symptoms of postnatal depression can begin during pregnancy, soon after birth, or up to a year after the baby is born.

whyNot.0: 2 weeks is the usual limit for baby blues, not depression.
whyNot.2: Depression can begin well after 6 weeks.
whyNot.3: Depression can begin later than 3 months.

explain.body: About 1 in 1,000 women. Sudden onset, usually in the first 2 weeks: hallucinations, delusions, mania, low or mixed mood, confusion. A medical emergency. Risk is higher with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, a family history or a previous episode. Refer for assessment within 4 hours; admission ideally to a mother and baby unit.

test.q: A woman admitted with postpartum psychosis 3 weeks after birth needs inpatient care. Where should she normally be admitted?
options: A general adult psychiatric ward
A postnatal ward in the maternity unit
A medical admissions unit
A specialist mother and baby unit
test.why: CG192 1.10.1: women who need inpatient care for a mental health problem within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit.

whyNot.0: A general ward may be used until an MBU bed is available, but the MBU is the recommended setting.
whyNot.1: A maternity ward cannot provide specialist psychiatric care.
whyNot.2: A medical unit is not a specialist mental health setting.
